playground.label: Check the links of a page: parse, resolve, deduplicate, read robots.txt and judge the status (offline stand-in answers)
playground.code:
from html.parser import HTMLParser from http import HTTPStatus from urllib.parse import urljoin, urldefrag, urlsplit, quote import urllib.robotparser as rp PAGE = '''

Books

fine broken elsewhere again mail no href

''' BASE = 'https://site.example/index.html' ANSWERS = {'https://site.example/ok.html': 200, 'https://site.example/gone.html': 404} # what a HEAD request would return class Links(HTMLParser): def __init__(self): super().__init__() self.hrefs = [] def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs): if tag == 'a': self.hrefs.append(dict(attrs).get('href')) p = Links() p.feed(PAGE) print('raw hrefs:', p.hrefs) seen = [] for h in p.hrefs: if not h: continue url = urldefrag(urljoin(BASE, h))[0] if urlsplit(url).scheme not in ('http', 'https'): continue if urlsplit(url).netloc != urlsplit(BASE).netloc: continue if url not in seen: seen.append(url) print('to check:', seen) robots = rp.RobotFileParser() robots.parse(['User-agent: *', 'Disallow: /private/']) for url in seen: status = ANSWERS[url] verdict = 'allowed' if robots.can_fetch('*', url) else 'disallowed by robots.txt' print(url, verdict, status, HTTPStatus(status).phrase, 'BROKEN' if status >= 400 else 'ok') print('https://www.openstreetmap.org/search?query=' + quote('777 Valencia St, San Francisco'))

findings: Background

Chapter 13 of the 3rd edition teaches how a program reaches the web in five steps of growing power: the webbrowser module that opens a page in the user's own browser, the requests module that downloads a page or a file, an API of a weather service answered in JSON, the parsing of HTML with Beautiful Soup, and the control of a real browser with Selenium and with Playwright; it builds three projects on them, showmap.py for OpenStreetMap, searchpypi.py for the search results of PyPI and downloadXkcdComics.py for a web comic, and closes with 18 practice questions and three practice programs, an image site downloader, the game 2048 and link verification.
Comparative analysis

The chapter's printed behaviours reproduce wherever they can run offline: the map URL of showmap.py with its address quoted, the status codes and the message of a failed download, the byte counts that write() returns while a response is saved in chunks, the conversion of 285.44 Kelvin to 12.3 Celsius and 54.1 Fahrenheit, and, with requests 2.34.2 and Beautiful Soup 4.15.0 run on the page that the chapter downloads, the matches, texts and attributes the chapter prints for the span with the id author and for the first two paragraphs; the page as downloaded and the book's own ontology agree byte for byte, since the SHA-256 of the chapter as fetched equals the digest the ontology records, and the file example3.html of 957 bytes has the SHA-256 c7a82b39 and Windows line ends.
Comparative analysis

Ten printed things in the chapter cannot be run as printed: the HTML of example3.html as typeset has a typographic quotation mark inside the href of the link, an unescaped p tag in the first paragraph and a misplaced closing form tag, so that on it Beautiful Soup 4.15.0 finds no element with the id author and eight paragraphs, whereas the file the chapter tells the reader to download has the escaped text and the right tags; the chapter says that select('p') gives a list of three matches, but the file has seven paragraphs, three of them inside the form; the file's alt text reads Close up where the chapter prints Close-up, and its title is Example Website Title where the chapter says that the Playwright program prints Example Website (the page's h1 is Example Website, and both Selenium and Playwright printed the title in real Firefox); the innerHTML that the chapter prints shows

where the browser returns <p>; the Step 4 listing of the comic downloader is indented with 8, 12, 15, 12 and then 6 spaces and Python rejects it with an IndentationError; the printed list of sys.argv shows the words St, and Francisco, with a trailing space that shell splitting never produces; the printed error of raise_for_status names a URL that ends in .html although the requested URL does not; the length of the Romeo and Juliet file printed as 178978 is 174126 today; and the command python3 -m playwright install is typeset with an en dash, which Python reads as a file name.
Comparative analysis

Two of the chapter's three projects meet today's web differently from the book, and one of them depends on the Python release: fetching the search page of PyPI with requests on 2026-10-12 returned status 200 with the page titled Client Challenge and no element of the class package-snippet, so searchpypi.py opens nothing; the robots.txt of pypi.org disallows /search*, a rule that RFC 9309 defines with the wildcard *, and urllib.robotparser matched it as a literal prefix and answered True for can_fetch up to Python 3.14.4, but from Python 3.14.5 (released 2026-05-10, gh-138907, support for RFC 9309) it answers False, so that the same check allowed the program on the five releases 3.14.0 to 3.14.4 and forbids it on 3.14.5 and 3.14.6; the XKCD page structure the chapter relies on still held on the same day, with the comic image inside the element with id comic at an address beginning with two slashes, a rel prev link and # as the href of the prev link of the first comic.
Comparative analysis

The chapter's advice on requests is correct and incomplete: raise_for_status() after every get() is what the library documents, but the documentation also says that nearly all production code should pass a timeout because a call without one can hang indefinitely (a call with timeout=0.2 raised ReadTimeout, and the same call without one returned the slow server's late answer), and that a download to a file should pass stream=True, because without it the whole body is read before get() returns (with stream=True the first five bytes were read while the server still held the rest), so that iter_content(100000) on a response fetched without stream=True only cuts an already loaded body into chunks.
Comparative analysis

What a program may fetch and with what identity is a question the chapter touches only through bandwidth, through the advice to prefer an API and through the secrecy of the key: the Robots Exclusion Protocol of RFC 9309 states that its rules are not a form of access authorization, so a robots.txt is a request that a polite crawler honours and the standard library can read with urllib.robotparser (which exposed Crawl-delay and Request-rate, and a crawler that read them waited between its pages); an API key identifies an account, the fake key of the chapter's example was answered by OpenWeather with status 401 and a JSON message on 2026-10-12, the free plan allows 60 calls a minute, and the weather service api.weather.gov, which the chapter names, answered with forecast periods and no key but documents that a User-Agent identifying the application is required.
Comparative analysis

The chapter's three practice programs were written and run against local stand-ins: link verification resolved relative links against the page URL, dropped the fragment so that a page linked twice counted once, skipped other sites and printed the one link that answered 404; an image site downloader saved the images of a results page with iter_content; and a crawler that read robots.txt first obeyed Crawl-delay and skipped a disallowed path; the game 2048 was not run, because it needs a browser on the live https site (the site answered 200 on 2026-10-12).
Conclusion

For an advanced course, chapter 13 is best taught as a choice of tool by the page in front of the program: webbrowser when the user should see the page, requests with raise_for_status and a timeout when the URL is known and the answer is text or a file, an API when the service offers one, Beautiful Soup on the text received when the page is static, and Selenium or Playwright only when the page needs a script or a login; the chapter's offline-checkable outputs hold, ten printed items do not run as printed, searchpypi.py meets a challenge page and a robots rule that changed meaning in Python 3.14.5, and what an advanced course adds is timeouts, streaming, robots.txt and its Python history, the newer Selenium and Playwright behaviour, the flags a browser reveals and the deprecations of current Python.
Contemporary developments

Current Python replaces or fences several details the chapter uses: PurePath.as_uri() is deprecated since Python 3.14 and removed in 3.19 in favour of Path.as_uri(), which gives the file:// URLs that the chapter suggests for local help pages; datetime.utcfromtimestamp() has been deprecated since 3.12, and datetime.fromtimestamp(), which the chapter names for the dt field of the forecast, answers in the local time zone of the machine, so the same timestamp printed 17:13 with the zone set to Europe/Istanbul and 07:13 with America/Los_Angeles; webbrowser.open() returns True or False and in 3.14 the BROWSER variable can name an already registered browser; and urllib.request.pathname2url has gained add_scheme in 3.14.
Contemporary developments

The Selenium part of the chapter was executed in a real Firefox 157 with Selenium 4.51.0 and is one step behind the library: Selenium Manager, shipped with every Selenium release, downloaded and found the driver and the browser by itself, so the manual geckodriver download and the webdriver-manager package that the chapter mentions were not needed; the exception the chapter calls NoSuchElement is NoSuchElementException; the text of a WebElement comes from the WebDriver command GET_ELEMENT_TEXT and is not the innerText property that the chapter calls its source (for an element hidden with display none the text was an empty string while the innerText property was secret, and for an element styled with text-transform the text and the innerText were capitalised while textContent was not); get_attribute looks for a property first and then for an attribute; the chapter's claim that a Selenium-driven browser has the user agent of a regular browser held (Firefox/157.0), but the browser also reported navigator.webdriver as True, a flag a page can read; and find_element_by_id of older tutorials no longer exists in Selenium 4.51.0.
Contemporary developments

The Playwright part was executed in a real Firefox 155 with Playwright 1.63.0 and is accurate: the chapter's first program printed the title, goto() returned the Response whose repr the chapter shows, the six locators of Table 13-5 each found their element on the example page, locators are strict (inner_text() on a locator of seven paragraphs raised a strict mode violation, which is why the chapter picks one with nth(0)), a click on a mistyped selector waited 30 seconds and raised TimeoutError while is_visible() and query_selector() answered at once, click() toggled a checkbox where check(), uncheck() and set_checked() set it, a Locator has no submit method, End and Home scrolled the page, Control+A selected the text of the page, and a headed launch without a display failed with a message about the missing XServer; the browsers are installed by a second step, playwright install, whose dry run lists Chrome for Testing, Chrome Headless Shell, Firefox, WebKit and FFmpeg.
Contemporary developments

A page built by a script shows why the chapter keeps a second family of tools: on a local page whose only paragraph is written by JavaScript, requests returned the script and an empty element, Beautiful Soup found the element with no text, and Selenium and Playwright in Firefox returned the written text; the chapter's advice to prefer a site's API holds on the day, since the NWS API returned fourteen forecast periods in JSON for the chapter's latitude and longitude while the forecast page of weather.gov that the chapter inspects still carried fourteen elements of the class forecast-text.
title: Web scraping for an advanced course: chapter 13 and today's web

nodes.label: Protocol
nodes.body: Chapter 13 starts from a plain fact: every tool in it, from a one-line webbrowser call to a driven Firefox, ends up sending a request to a web address and reading what comes back, and the chapter's first section, HTTP and HTTPS, explains the address and the protocol (Sweigart, 2025). A program that does this is a guest on someone else's computer, and that adds questions of manners that a reader of the book does not meet until a site says no.

paras.text: Chapter 13 starts from a plain fact: every tool in it, from a one-line webbrowser call to a driven Firefox, ends up sending a request to a web address and reading what comes back, and the chapter's first section, HTTP and HTTPS, explains the address and the protocol (Sweigart, 2025). A program that does this is a guest on someone else's computer, and that adds questions of manners that a reader of the book does not meet until a site says no.

Three ideas carry this subject. Address forms covers how a URL is cut into scheme, host, path, query and fragment, and how the characters in it are written. Protocol basics covers HTTPS, the status codes of the answer and the user agent a request announces. Crawler manners covers what a site asks of programs that visit it, in its robots.txt, and the pace a polite program keeps.

nodes.label: Address forms
nodes.body: The web address is the first thing every program of the chapter needs, and the chapter reads two of them closely: the OpenStreetMap search address of Project 6 and the OpenWeather endpoint of the weather section (Sweigart, 2025). Both are URLs, a string with a fixed grammar that a program can take apart and put together without guessing.

paras.text: The web address is the first thing every program of the chapter needs, and the chapter reads two of them closely: the OpenStreetMap search address of Project 6 and the OpenWeather endpoint of the weather section (Sweigart, 2025). Both are URLs, a string with a fixed grammar that a program can take apart and put together without guessing.

Url anatomy covers the five parts of a URL and the function that splits them. Query string covers the part after the question mark, which carries the names and values a service asks for. Percent encoding covers how a space or a comma is written so that it survives the trip. Fragment part covers the end of a URL that never leaves the browser.

nodes.label: Url anatomy
nodes.body: The chapter breaks https://api.openweathermap.org/geo/1.0/direct?q={city_name},{state_code},{country_code}&appid={API_key} into the scheme https://, the domain name api.openweathermap.org, the path /geo/1.0/direct and the query string that follows the question mark (Sweigart, 2025). RFC 3986 gives the general grammar behind it: a scheme, an authority, a path, an optional query and an optional fragment (Internet Engineering Task Force, 2005).

paras.text: The chapter breaks https://api.openweathermap.org/geo/1.0/direct?q={city_name},{state_code},{country_code}&appid={API_key} into the scheme https://, the domain name api.openweathermap.org, the path /geo/1.0/direct and the query string that follows the question mark (Sweigart, 2025). RFC 3986 gives the general grammar behind it: a scheme, an authority, a path, an optional query and an optional fragment (Internet Engineering Task Force, 2005).

Think of a postal address: country, city, street, then the flat number. Under Python 3.14.6, urllib.parse.urlsplit cut the chapter's URL into ('https', 'api.openweathermap.org', '/geo/1.0/direct', 'q=San,CA,US&appid=KEY') for its first four parts (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The fifth part, the fragment, is the subject of Fragment part, and the query is taken apart in Query string.

nodes.definition: A URL is written as a scheme, a host, a path, an optional query after a question mark and an optional fragment after a number sign; urllib.parse.urlsplit cuts it into those parts.

io.code: __import__('urllib.parse', fromlist=['x']).urlsplit('https://api.openweathermap.org/geo/1.0/direct?q=San,CA,US&appid=KEY')[:4]

nodes.label: Query string
nodes.body: The chapter explains that in URL encoding the parameter name and the argument value are separated by an equal sign and that several pairs are separated by an ampersand, and it fills the pairs from variables with an f-string (Sweigart, 2025). The query string is how a program tells a service what it wants: which city, which key.

paras.text: The chapter explains that in URL encoding the parameter name and the argument value are separated by an equal sign and that several pairs are separated by an ampersand, and it fills the pairs from variables with an f-string (Sweigart, 2025). The query string is how a program tells a service what it wants: which city, which key.

Under Python 3.14.6, parse_qs('q=San+Francisco%2CCA&appid=KEY') returned {'q': ['San Francisco,CA'], 'appid': ['KEY']}, a dictionary of lists because a name may repeat, and urlencode({'q': 'San Francisco,CA,US', 'appid': 'KEY'}) wrote 'q=San+Francisco%2CCA%2CUS&appid=KEY' (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The chapter as read does not present these two functions, and writes the query by hand; Percent encoding explains the plus sign and the %2C in that output.

nodes.definition: The query string of a URL is a list of name=value pairs joined by ampersands; parse_qs reads the pairs back into a dictionary of lists and turns a plus sign or a percent code back into the character.

io.code: __import__('urllib.parse', fromlist=['x']).parse_qs('q=San+Francisco%2CCA&appid=KEY')

nodes.label: Percent encoding
nodes.body: The chapter notes that the browser handles necessary URL encoding by itself, such as turning a space into %20 (Sweigart, 2025). Percent-encoding is the rule behind that: a character that a URL may not carry is written as a percent sign and the two hexadecimal digits of its byte, so that a space becomes %20 and a comma %2C.

paras.text: The chapter notes that the browser handles necessary URL encoding by itself, such as turning a space into %20 (Sweigart, 2025). Percent-encoding is the rule behind that: a character that a URL may not carry is written as a percent sign and the two hexadecimal digits of its byte, so that a space becomes %20 and a comma %2C.

A program that builds a URL has to do what the browser does. Under Python 3.14.6, quote('777 Valencia St, San Francisco, CA 94110') gave '777%20Valencia%20St%2C%20San%20Francisco%2C%20CA%2094110', the very text that OpenStreetMap shows in its address bar (Python Software Foundation, 2026). quote('a/b c') keeps the slash and gives 'a/b%20c', quote('a/b c', safe='') gives 'a%2Fb%20c', and quote_plus writes a space as a plus; Show map program shows why an ampersand in an address needs this.

nodes.example: %20 for a space, %2C for a comma
nodes.definition: Percent-encoding writes a character that a URL may not carry as a percent sign and two hexadecimal digits, a space as %20 and a comma as %2C; urllib.parse.quote does it for a program, as the browser does for the address typed into its bar.

io.code: __import__('urllib.parse', fromlist=['x']).quote('777 Valencia St, San Francisco, CA 94110')

nodes.label: Fragment part
nodes.body: The OpenStreetMap address that the chapter copies from the address bar ends in #map=19/37.75897/-122.42142, and the chapter tests that the part after the number sign can be removed and the page still loads (Sweigart, 2025). That part is the fragment: it names a place inside the page, here the zoom level and the map centre, and the browser uses it, the server does not receive it.

paras.text: The OpenStreetMap address that the chapter copies from the address bar ends in #map=19/37.75897/-122.42142, and the chapter tests that the part after the number sign can be removed and the page still loads (Sweigart, 2025). That part is the fragment: it names a place inside the page, here the zoom level and the map centre, and the browser uses it, the server does not receive it.

RFC 3986 defines the fragment as a way to identify a secondary resource by reference to the primary one (Internet Engineering Task Force, 2005). Under Python 3.14.6, urlsplit returned map=19/37.75897/-122.42142 as the fragment of the chapter's address, and a request that urllib sent to a local server for a URL with a fragment reached the server as '/search?query=777%20Valencia' with the fragment gone (Python Software Foundation, 2026). A fragment is therefore invisible to requests-based scraping, which is one more reason to read Query string first.

nodes.definition: The fragment of a URL, after the number sign, names a place inside the page and is handled by the browser; it is not sent to the server, which is why the chapter can cut it from the OpenStreetMap address and still load the page.

io.code: __import__('urllib.parse', fromlist=['x']).urlsplit('https://www.openstreetmap.org/search?query=777%20Valencia%20St%2C%20San%20Francisco%2C%20CA%2094110#map=19/37.75897/-122.42142')[3:]

nodes.label: Protocol basics
nodes.body: Once the address is understood, the chapter says what the program talks to the server in: HTTP, in its encrypted form HTTPS, and a server answers every request with a status code (Sweigart, 2025). Every later check of the chapter, from raise_for_status to the empty list of a failed search, rests on these answers.

paras.text: Once the address is understood, the chapter says what the program talks to the server in: HTTP, in its encrypted form HTTPS, and a server answers every request with a status code (Sweigart, 2025). Every later check of the chapter, from raise_for_status to the empty list of a failed search, rests on these answers.

Https encryption covers what the encryption protects and what it still shows. Status code covers the three digits that begin every answer and the classes they fall into. User agent covers the name a request gives itself, which a server can use to tell a script from a browser.

nodes.label: Https encryption
nodes.body: The chapter explains that HTTPS is an encrypted version of HTTP, so that identity thieves, national intelligence agencies or an internet service provider cannot view the pages visited or the passwords and card numbers submitted; a VPN only moves that visibility to the VPN provider, and the identity of the website visited can still be known (Sweigart, 2025). Most sites now encrypt all traffic, not just the pages with a password.

paras.text: The chapter explains that HTTPS is an encrypted version of HTTP, so that identity thieves, national intelligence agencies or an internet service provider cannot view the pages visited or the passwords and card numbers submitted; a VPN only moves that visibility to the VPN provider, and the identity of the website visited can still be known (Sweigart, 2025). Most sites now encrypt all traffic, not just the pages with a password.

Encryption is a sealed envelope: the post office sees the two addresses but not the letter. This build did not capture network traffic, so the claim rests on the chapter. What it did meet is the trust half of the story: requests reached https sites through the build proxy only because its certificate authority was supplied in a CA bundle, and the Firefox started for this chapter, which did not have that authority, could not open the live https sites. An encrypted connection protects against everyone except a party the client chooses to trust, which is the chapter's point about VPN providers in a different place.

nodes.definition: HTTPS is HTTP over an encrypted connection: the content of the pages and what is submitted are hidden from the network, but the name of the site visited can still be seen.

nodes.label: Status code

nodes.label: Robots txt
nodes.body: The chapter as read never mentions robots.txt. RFC 9309 defines it as a plain-text file at the root of a site whose rules crawlers are requested to honour, and states that these rules are not a form of access authorization (Internet Engineering Task Force, 2022). It is a notice on the gate, not a lock on it.

paras.text: The chapter as read never mentions robots.txt. RFC 9309 defines it as a plain-text file at the root of a site whose rules crawlers are requested to honour, and states that these rules are not a form of access authorization (Internet Engineering Task Force, 2022). It is a notice on the gate, not a lock on it.

urllib.robotparser reads such a file. Under Python 3.14.6, with the rules User-agent: * and Disallow: /search*, can_fetch was False for https://pypi.org/search/?q=boring+stuff and True for a project page, and the real robots.txt of pypi.org of 2026-10-12, with twelve Disallow lines among them /simple/, /search* and /account/, gave False for the search page of searchpypi.py (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Up to Python 3.14.4 the same rule gave True, because the module matched the path as a literal prefix; the 3.14.5 release of 2026-05-10 added support for RFC 9309 (gh-138907) and its wildcard * and end mark $ (Python Software Foundation, 2026). The robots.txt of xkcd.com disallows /personal/ for every agent and the whole site for GPTBot, so the comic downloader may fetch comic pages. Challenge page continues with what PyPI answered instead.

nodes.definition: A robots.txt file at the root of a site lists the paths that crawlers are asked not to fetch; it is a request and not an access control, urllib.robotparser reads it and answers can_fetch, and since Python 3.14.5 it reads the wildcard * and the end mark $ of RFC 9309.

Its example is rj.txt, the whole of Romeo and Juliet.

nodes.label: Request timeout
nodes.body: The chapter as read never mentions a timeout. The requests documentation says that a timeout in seconds tells it to stop waiting, and that nearly all production code should use the parameter in nearly all requests, because without it a program can hang indefinitely (Requests documentation, 2026). A call such as requests.get(url, timeout=10) is the cure.

paras.text: The chapter as read never mentions a timeout. The requests documentation says that a timeout in seconds tells it to stop waiting, and that nearly all production code should use the parameter in nearly all requests, because without it a program can hang indefinitely (Requests documentation, 2026). A call such as requests.get(url, timeout=10) is the cure.

It is the difference between waiting at a counter for a minute and waiting for ever. Against a local server that held its answer for a second, requests.get(url, timeout=0.2) raised ReadTimeout, a subclass of Timeout and of RequestException, while the same call without a timeout returned the late answer; urllib under Python 3.14.6 raised TimeoutError in under half a second for urlopen(url, timeout=0.2) and returned b'late' when called without one (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Raise for status does not help here: it judges an answer, and a hung call has none.

nodes.definition: A call of requests.get without a timeout argument waits for ever for a server that does not answer; the timeout argument, in seconds, makes it raise a Timeout exception instead, and the documentation asks for it in nearly all production code.

A local server answered status 200 and requests.codes.ok == 200; the list [(200, True), (301, True), (404, False), (500, False)] is what the rule gives. The service's API, its application programming interface, is the specification that says how to ask.

nodes.label: Polite crawler
nodes.body: The chapter limits its downloads to ten and sleeps one second per page, and does not mention that a site publishes its own rules for crawlers (Sweigart, 2025). A polite crawler adds one step at the start: read robots.txt, skip what it disallows and wait what it asks.

A crawler written for this chapter fetched robots.txt from a local server first, read Crawl-delay: 1 and a rule Disallow: /private, followed links from /a to /b and /c, skipped /private/x without fetching it, and took at least three seconds for its three pages, using requests, bs4 and urllib.robotparser (Requests documentation, 2026) (Python Software Foundation, 2026). Robots txt and Polite delay explain each piece; none of them is enforced by the server, only by the crawler's own conduct.

nodes.definition: A crawler that wants to be polite reads the robots.txt of the site first, skips the paths it disallows and waits the Crawl-delay between pages, which the standard library hands to the program.

nodes.body: Requests and Beautiful Soup work as long as the program can work out the URL of the page it wants and that page already contains the data. When the URL is hard to find, the page is built by a script, or the site wants a login, the chapter turns to a program that starts a real browser and drives it as a user does: first Selenium, then the newer Playwright (Sweigart, 2025).

Five ideas carry this subject. Selenium driver covers starting the browser and clicking its buttons. Selenium elements covers finding, reading and operating the elements of a page. Playwright driver covers the synchronous form, headless mode and the browser buttons. Playwright elements covers locators, waiting, checkboxes and keys. Tool choice covers when a driven browser is the right tool and what it gives away.

nodes.label: Element lookup
nodes.body: find_element() returns a single WebElement, the first match, and find_elements() returns a list of WebElements, one for every match; if nothing matches, Selenium raises an exception that the chapter calls NoSuchElement, which the program can catch with try and except (Sweigart, 2025).

In Selenium 4.51.0 the library has NoSuchElementException and no NoSuchElement; a real Firefox raised it for By.ID 'nope' with the message Unable to locate element: [id='nope'] and a link to the documentation, while find_elements returned [] for the same locator (Selenium documentation, 2026). The method find_element_by_id of older tutorials no longer exists on the driver. Playwright decides differently, as Auto waiting explains.

nodes.definition: find_element returns the first matching WebElement and raises NoSuchElementException when there is none, while find_elements returns a list that is empty when there is none.

nodes.label: Element properties
nodes.body: Table 13-4 lists tag_name, get_attribute, get_property, text, clear, is_displayed, is_enabled, is_selected, location and size, and the chapter says that text is a shortcut for get_property('innerText'), with innerText and innerHTML as properties rather than attributes (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Table 13-4 lists tag_name, get_attribute, get_property, text, clear, is_displayed, is_enabled, is_selected, location and size, and the chapter says that text is a shortcut for get_property('innerText'), with innerText and innerHTML as properties rather than attributes (Sweigart, 2025).

All of the table's names exist in Selenium 4.51.0. In Firefox the first paragraph of the example page gave the text 'This

tag puts content into a single paragraph.' and the innerHTML 'This <p> tag puts content into a single paragraph.', and the checkbox was displayed and enabled but not selected before a click and selected after. The text, though, is read by the WebDriver command Get Element Text and its source does not mention innerText: for an element hidden with display none the text was an empty string while the innerText property was 'secret', and for an element styled with text-transform both were capitalised while textContent kept the page's letters (Selenium documentation, 2026). Size has the keys height and width, and location x and y.

nodes.definition: A WebElement gives its rendered text in text, its source through get_property('innerHTML'), a property or attribute through get_attribute, and whether it is displayed, enabled or selected; the text of an element hidden from view is empty.

nodes.label: Click and submit
nodes.body: click() simulates a mouse click on an element, which follows a link, picks a radio button or presses a Submit button, and send_keys() types into an input or textarea; submit() on any element of a form acts as the Submit button of that form (Sweigart, 2025). The chapter fills the fake login of the example page and warns against putting passwords in source code.

paras.text: click() simulates a mouse click on an element, which follows a link, picks a radio button or presses a Submit button, and send_keys() types into an input or textarea; submit() on any element of a form acts as the Submit button of that form (Sweigart, 2025). The chapter fills the fake login of the example page and warns against putting passwords in source code.

In Firefox 157, clicking the link by By.LINK_TEXT took the browser to the page it names; send_keys put your_real_username_here into the field whose placeholder is admin, and the password field's type was password; submit() sent the form, which changed the address (Browser buttons) (Selenium documentation, 2026). The chapter's own example is a fake login that goes nowhere; a real login belongs to the key habits of Access key, a file and not the source.

nodes.definition: click follows a link or presses a button, send_keys types into a field, and submit sends the form that contains the element; the login fields of the chapter's page are found by id, and a password belongs in a file, not in the source.

nodes.label: Special keys
nodes.body: Selenium represents keyboard keys in selenium.webdriver.common.keys, imported as Keys, and send_keys accepts Keys.ENTER, RETURN, HOME, END, PAGE_UP, PAGE_DOWN, UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT, TAB, ESCAPE, BACK_SPACE, DELETE and F1 to F12; with the cursor in no text field, END and HOME scroll the page to its bottom and top (Sweigart, 2025). Sending them to the html element is the chapter's trick.

Sending them to the html element is the chapter's trick.

Keys.ENTER is the character '\ue007', Keys.HOME '\ue011' and Keys.END '\ue010'. On a local page of thirty tall rows, Keys.END sent to the html element scrolled the page down and Keys.HOME brought scrollY back to 0, and eight arrow-key presses sent to the body reached the page's script as ArrowUp, ArrowRight, ArrowDown, ArrowLeft twice over (Selenium documentation, 2026). These are the keys that Game keystrokes needs, and Fill and press sends the same with Playwright.

nodes.definition: send_keys also takes the constants of Keys, such as Keys.END and Keys.HOME, which scroll the page when the cursor is in no field, and the arrow keys, which reach the script of a page.

nodes.label: Playwright driver
nodes.body: Playwright is a browser-controlling library similar to Selenium, but newer, with some features that merit learning, headless mode first among them, and its drivers are installed with one command (Sweigart, 2025). The chapter does not repeat the general scraping and selector material it gave for Selenium.

paras.text: Playwright is a browser-controlling library similar to Selenium, but newer, with some features that merit learning, headless mode first among them, and its drivers are installed with one command (Sweigart, 2025). The chapter does not repeat the general scraping and selector material it gave for Selenium.

Sync playwright covers the first program and the with block. Headless mode covers running without a window and the way to watch. Playwright buttons covers the four Page methods that click the browser's buttons.

nodes.label: Sync playwright
nodes.body: The chapter's first Playwright program is from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright, a with block, playwright.firefox.launch(), browser.new_page(), page.goto(url), print(page.title()) and browser.close(); the with block calls start() and stop() for the program, and the synchronous mode means a function does not return until its operation is complete, so the program cannot ask for an element before the page has loaded (Sweigart, 2025). The asynchronous features are beyond the book's scope.

paras.text: The chapter's first Playwright program is from playwright.sync_api import sync_playwright, a with block, playwright.firefox.launch(), browser.new_page(), page.goto(url), print(page.title()) and browser.close(); the with block calls start() and stop() for the program, and the synchronous mode means a function does not return until its operation is complete, so the program cannot ask for an element before the page has loaded (Sweigart, 2025). The asynchronous features are beyond the book's scope.

In a real Firefox 155 with Playwright 1.63.0 the program ran as written against a local copy of the example page, and printed the title Example Website Title, where the chapter says it prints Example Website, which is the heading and not the title (Playwright documentation, 2026). goto returned a Response whose repr has the shape the chapter shows, <Response url=... request=<Request url=... method='GET'>>. playwright.chromium.launch() and webkit.launch(), the chapter's other two engines, were not started.

nodes.definition: Playwright is used in its synchronous form inside a with block, which starts and stops it; the block launches a browser, makes a page and closes both, and the page methods return when the operation is complete.

nodes.label: Headless mode
nodes.body: Playwright runs a browser in headless mode by default, without a window, which the chapter says makes it useful for automated tests and scraping in the background; to watch, the interactive shell form starts the browser with launch(headless=False, slow_mo=50), which shows the window and adds a 50 ms delay to each operation, and ends with browser.close() and playwright.stop() (Sweigart, 2025). The browsers themselves are installed with python -m playwright install, written in the chapter for macOS and Linux as python3 –m with an en dash.

The browsers themselves are installed with python -m playwright install, written in the chapter for macOS and Linux as python3 –m with an en dash.

On this machine, which has no display, a headed launch failed at once with a message about launching a headed browser without an XServer; python3 with an en dash before m was read by Python as a file name and stopped with 'can't open file' and exit code 2. playwright install --dry-run listed what the command would fetch: Chrome for Testing, Chrome Headless Shell, Firefox 155, WebKit and FFmpeg (Playwright documentation, 2026). Sync playwright runs headless unless told otherwise.

nodes.definition: A browser launched by Playwright runs headless by default, without a window, and headless=False with slow_mo shows the steps; a headed launch needs a display, and the browsers are installed with the command playwright install.

nodes.label: Playwright buttons
nodes.body: page.go_back() clicks the Back button, go_forward() the Forward button, reload() the Refresh button and close() the Close Window button, as Page methods on the object that browser.new_page() returns; a Page is a new tab in a new browser window, and several can be open at once (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: page.go_back() clicks the Back button, go_forward() the Forward button, reload() the Refresh button and close() the Close Window button, as Page methods on the object that browser.new_page() returns; a Page is a new tab in a new browser window, and several can be open at once (Sweigart, 2025).

In Firefox 155, clicking the Submit button of the example page changed the address to the page followed by a question mark, go_back() returned to the address without it, go_forward() to the one with it, and reload() kept the title Example Website Title (Playwright documentation, 2026). Browser buttons lists the Selenium names for the same four actions.

nodes.definition: Playwright clicks the buttons of the browser with the Page methods go_back, go_forward, reload and close, and goto loads a URL and returns the Response.

nodes.label: Playwright elements
nodes.body: Playwright finds an element with a locator, a method of the Page that returns a Locator object standing for the elements that may match, and acts on it with the methods of Table 13-6 (Sweigart, 2025). A locator is a standing order for 'the element that looks like this', placed with the shop but filled when the page is ready.

paras.text: Playwright finds an element with a locator, a method of the Page that returns a Locator object standing for the elements that may match, and acts on it with the methods of Table 13-6 (Sweigart, 2025). A locator is a standing order for 'the element that looks like this', placed with the shop but filled when the page is ready.

Page locators covers the six locators of Table 13-5. Locator methods covers Table 13-6 and the strictness of a locator. Auto waiting covers the 30-second pause. Check boxes covers the difference between click and check. Fill and press covers typing and keys.

nodes.label: Page locators
nodes.body: Table 13-5 lists get_by_role, get_by_text, get_by_label, get_by_placeholder, get_by_alt_text and locator; the chapter explains roles as the ARIA standards that let software identify content for users with vision or other disabilities, such as the heading role for h1 to h6, and locates the link with get_by_text('is a link'), the checkbox with get_by_label('Agree'), the field with get_by_placeholder('admin') and the picture with get_by_alt_text('Zophie') (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: Table 13-5 lists get_by_role, get_by_text, get_by_label, get_by_placeholder, get_by_alt_text and locator; the chapter explains roles as the ARIA standards that let software identify content for users with vision or other disabilities, such as the heading role for h1 to h6, and locates the link with get_by_text('is a link'), the checkbox with get_by_label('Agree'), the field with get_by_placeholder('admin') and the picture with get_by_alt_text('Zophie') (Sweigart, 2025).

In Firefox 155 each of them found its element on the example page: get_by_role('checkbox') one input, get_by_role('heading', name='Example Website') one h1, get_by_text('is a link') one a, get_by_label('Agree') one input, get_by_placeholder('admin') one input, get_by_alt_text('Zophie') one img, and locator('p') seven p elements (Playwright documentation, 2026). MDN describes the heading role as defining an element as a heading to a page or section (MDN Web Docs, 2026). Locator methods shows what these locators can do.

nodes.definition: A Page offers get_by_role, get_by_text, get_by_label, get_by_placeholder, get_by_alt_text and locator for a CSS or XPath selector, each returning a Locator that stands for the elements that may match.

nodes.label: Locator methods
nodes.body: Table 13-6 lists get_attribute, count, nth, first, last, all, inner_text, inner_html, click, is_visible, is_enabled, is_checked and bounding_box, and the chapter's program picks the first paragraph of the page with page.locator('p') and nth(0) (Sweigart, 2025). A Locator may stand for many elements, and nth gives it one.

paras.text: Table 13-6 lists get_attribute, count, nth, first, last, all, inner_text, inner_html, click, is_visible, is_enabled, is_checked and bounding_box, and the chapter's program picks the first paragraph of the page with page.locator('p') and nth(0) (Sweigart, 2025). A Locator may stand for many elements, and nth gives it one.

All of them exist on the Locator of Playwright 1.63.0. In Firefox 155 the program printed the text and the inner HTML of the first paragraph, count() was 7, first agreed with nth(0), last read 'Agree to disagree: ', and all() returned seven Locators; inner_text() on the locator of seven paragraphs raised an Error beginning strict mode violation, because a Locator is strict and an action on several elements is refused, which is why the chapter picks one with nth(0) (Playwright documentation, 2026). bounding_box() had the keys height, width, x and y, and is_visible() on the id author was True and on a missing id False.

nodes.definition: A Locator counts its matches, picks one with nth, first or last, reads inner_text and inner_html, and acts with click, fill, press, check and uncheck; it is strict, so an action on a locator that matches several elements raises an error.

nodes.label: Auto waiting
nodes.body: Because Playwright understands that a page might create an element later, it pauses for 30 seconds while it waits for an element that does not exist to appear, and the chapter gives is_visible() on a Locator and page.query_selector() as the checks that answer at once, query_selector returning None when the element is not there (Sweigart, 2025). Selenium, by contrast, raises an error at once.

paras.text: Because Playwright understands that a page might create an element later, it pauses for 30 seconds while it waits for an element that does not exist to appear, and the chapter gives is_visible() on a Locator and page.query_selector() as the checks that answer at once, query_selector returning None when the element is not there (Sweigart, 2025). Selenium, by contrast, raises an error at once.

The Playwright documentation says an action auto-waits for its actionability checks and fails with TimeoutError if they do not pass within the timeout, whose default in Playwright 1.63.0 is 30000 milliseconds (Playwright documentation, 2026). In Firefox 155 a click on the misspelled '#login_usr' waited 30 seconds and raised TimeoutError, is_visible() on it returned False and query_selector() returned None in under a second, and click(timeout=500) failed after 0.6 seconds. Element lookup showed the other design.

nodes.definition: Playwright waits for an element to exist and be ready before it acts, up to a default timeout of 30 seconds, so a mistyped selector makes the program pause that long; is_visible and query_selector answer at once.

nodes.label: Check boxes
nodes.body: The Page methods click(), check(), uncheck() and set_checked() simulate clicks on links, buttons and checkboxes; click toggles a checkbox to the opposite state, whereas check and uncheck leave it checked or unchecked whatever it was before, and set_checked takes True or False, so the chapter calls check and uncheck more reliable (Sweigart, 2025).

paras.text: The Page methods click(), check(), uncheck() and set_checked() simulate clicks on links, buttons and checkboxes; click toggles a checkbox to the opposite state, whereas check and uncheck leave it checked or unchecked whatever it was before, and set_checked takes True or False, so the chapter calls check and uncheck more reliable (Sweigart, 2025).

In Firefox 155 two click() calls on the checkbox of the example page gave the states [True, False], so each call toggled it; check() twice gave True, uncheck() twice gave False, and set_checked(True) and set_checked(False) gave True and False (Playwright documentation, 2026). The difference matters when a program does not know the state it starts from, which the page may have saved.

nodes.definition: click toggles a checkbox to the opposite of its state, while check, uncheck and set_checked leave it checked or unchecked whatever it was before, which is why the chapter calls them more reliable.

nodes.label: Fill and press
nodes.body: A Locator's fill() types a string into an input or textarea, clear() erases it, and press() sends a key to the element, either a single character, a modifier such as Control+A, or a name such as End, Home, ArrowUp or Enter; unlike Selenium, there is no submit() and the Submit button is clicked (Sweigart, 2025). The chapter fills the example page's fake login.

paras.text: A Locator's fill() types a string into an input or textarea, clear() erases it, and press() sends a key to the element, either a single character, a modifier such as Control+A, or a name such as End, Home, ArrowUp or Enter; unlike Selenium, there is no submit() and the Submit button is clicked (Sweigart, 2025). The chapter fills the example page's fake login.

In Firefox 155 fill put your_real_username_here and your_real_password_here into the two fields, clear() left an empty string, hasattr(Locator, 'submit') was False, and clicking input[type=submit] changed the address as the Selenium submit did; End scrolled the tall page down and Home brought scrollY back to 0, Control+A selected more than 100 characters of the page, and eight arrow-key presses reached the page's script in order (Playwright documentation, 2026). Special keys shows the Selenium counterpart.

nodes.definition: fill types text into an input or textarea, clear erases it, and press sends a key such as End or Control+A to the element; there is no submit method, so the Submit button is clicked.

nodes.label: Tool choice
nodes.body: The question under the whole chapter is which tool the page in front of the program needs: a browser launcher, a downloader and parser, or a driven browser (Sweigart, 2025). The chapter gives its answer in the first lines of its Selenium section and again in the Summary.

paras.text: The question under the whole chapter is which tool the page in front of the program needs: a browser launcher, a downloader and parser, or a driven browser (Sweigart, 2025). The chapter gives its answer in the first lines of its Selenium section and again in the Summary.
Dynamic pages covers when the text a download receives is not the page. Automation tells covers what a site can learn about a driven browser.

nodes.label: Dynamic pages
nodes.body: The chapter says that a page that depends on JavaScript that updates it, or that needs a login, calls for Selenium and not requests, that large sites recognise scripts and may refuse them, that a driven browser is more likely to work on those sites but slower and hard to run in the background, and that an API is the better choice when the site offers one (Sweigart, 2025). The tool is chosen by where the data is built.

The tool is chosen by where the data is built.

On a local page whose only paragraph is written by JavaScript, requests returned the script and an empty element, Beautiful Soup found the element with no text, and Selenium and Playwright in Firefox returned the written text, Built by a script, not in the source (Requests documentation, 2026) (Playwright documentation, 2026). The Client Challenge page of Challenge page is the real example of a page that a plain download cannot pass, and Weather services is the API route that the chapter prefers.

nodes.definition: A page whose content is built by scripts, or that needs a login, cannot be read from the text requests downloads; the program then needs a browser driver, which is slower, and an API is preferable whenever the service offers one.

nodes.label: Automation tells
nodes.body: The chapter says that a major tell to websites that you are using a script is the user-agent string, that a Selenium-driven browser has the same user agent as a regular browser, and that it downloads images, advertisements, cookies and trackers like a regular browser, but that websites can still find ways to detect Selenium and major ticketing and e-commerce sites often block it (Sweigart, 2025). A driven browser is a person in a costume, and the costume has seams.

paras.text: The chapter says that a major tell to websites that you are using a script is the user-agent string, that a Selenium-driven browser has the same user agent as a regular browser, and that it downloads images, advertisements, cookies and trackers like a regular browser, but that websites can still find ways to detect Selenium and major ticketing and e-commerce sites often block it (Sweigart, 2025). A driven browser is a person in a costume, and the costume has seams.

In Firefox 157 driven by Selenium the user agent ended in Firefox/157.0, as a regular browser's does, while requests had sent python-requests; yet the page itself could read navigator.webdriver, which was True (Selenium documentation, 2026). That flag is one of the seams a page can see. Whether a script should hide it is a question of the site's rules, the subject of Robots txt.

nodes.definition: A site can recognise a script by its user-agent string and by flags that a driven browser reveals, such as navigator.webdriver, so a driven browser passes for human only in part and a ticketing or shopping site may still refuse it.

lecture.title: Chapter 13: Web Scraping
lecture.say: Welcome. This chapter follows a program from an address to a page it can read: the URL, the reply, the API, the HTML, and the browser it may have to drive. Every code slide shows the code, a plain explanation, and the result as a table, chart or diagram.

lecture.title: Today's route
lecture.say: Five parts: addresses and manners, opening and downloading, a weather API, reading HTML, and driving a browser. Each code slide has its place in the chapter-code tab of the page, in this same order.

lecture.title: Two questions this chapter answers
lecture.say: Two questions to carry through the chapter. Which tool reaches which kind of page, and what decides the choice? And which printed outputs and programs of the book differ in current Python and on today's web?

lecture.title: Part 1: Addresses and manners
lecture.say: Part one. Before any download: an address has parts, a reply has a status code, a program has a name, and a site can say which paths it would rather not be crawled. Predict each answer before you read the result.

lecture.title: Everyday pictures: addresses and manners
lecture.say: A postal address is a good picture for a URL. HTTP is a postcard, HTTPS a sealed envelope. Ask students to add one more picture of their own.

lecture.title: A URL is a scheme, a host, a path, a query and a fragment
lecture.say: A URL is not one string but five parts. Urlsplit names them. Predict which part the server never receives, then check the fragment row.

lecture.title: Percent codes and the query string
lecture.say: A space and a comma may not stand in an address. Quote writes them as percent codes, parse_qs reads them back. Predict the encoded text before you run.

lecture.title: HTTP status codes: the first digit is the class
lecture.say: The first digit of a status code is its class: two for success, three for redirection, four for the client's fault, five for the server's. Which class is a 429?

lecture.title: The user agent tells a server who is asking
lecture.say: Python's downloader announces itself as Python-urllib, and a site may refuse it. A polite program sets its own name and a contact address.

lecture.title: robots.txt: the paths a crawler is asked to avoid
lecture.say: A robots.txt file lists paths a crawler is asked to avoid. The parser answers true or false. It is a request and not a lock, so honour it.

lecture.title: Story: a courtesy file for robots, 30 June 1994
lecture.say: Martijn Koster wrote down the consensus of 30 June 1994. The file is a courtesy, not a lock: the text itself says nobody enforces it. Ask students: what would you do if a site asked you not to crawl a path?

lecture.title: A polite crawler waits between pages
lecture.say: Some sites state a pause in their robots file. The fake clock shows the schedule without waiting. Predict the time of the third fetch.

lecture.title: Story: the first spider counted 130 sites, 1993
lecture.say: Matthew Gray built the first spider in 1993 to count the Web. 130 sites in June 1993, 100,000 by January 1996. Our link loop is the same idea at toy scale: fetch, find links, follow, repeat.

lecture.title: Part 2: Opening and downloading
lecture.say: Part two. Three ways to get at a page: ask the browser to show it, download it, or download it in chunks. The standard library stands in for requests so that every example runs on this page.

lecture.title: Everyday pictures: opening a page with webbrowser
lecture.say: The webbrowser module is the simplest tool of the chapter. It only opens a page in your own browser and cannot read it.

lecture.title: Everyday pictures: downloading with requests
lecture.say: Requests is the courier of the chapter. It brings the parcel, and raise_for_status reads the slip. Chunks let a huge parcel arrive box by box.

lecture.title: webbrowser.open asks your own browser to show a page
lecture.say: On this page the open call is replaced by a recorder so that no window opens. The real call returns true when a browser started and cannot read the page.

lecture.title: Project 6: a map address from the command line
lecture.say: Project six. The words typed after the script name become an address, which is percent-encoded and added to a search address. Predict the encoded text.

lecture.title: Fetching a page: the reply has a type and a body
lecture.say: A data address holds its text inside the address, so urlopen needs no network. The reply has a content type and a body of bytes.

lecture.title: Story: Requests, conceived in frustration, 13 February 2011
lecture.say: Requests was conceived on 13 February 2011 and born the next day. The version history still says Frustration, Conception, Birth. Ask students what frustrated him: network errors, routing and compression.

lecture.title: raise_for_status stops the program on a bad reply
lecture.say: Call raise_for_status after every download. A good reply passes quietly, a bad reply stops the program before it saves an error page as a file.

lecture.title: iter_content: save a download in chunks
lecture.say: Iter_content hands out a body in pieces. The write calls return the byte counts. Predict the last chunk, which is shorter.

lecture.title: Part 3: A weather API
lecture.say: Part three. A weather service answers in JSON. We read the reply, convert Kelvin, and build the address with a hidden key. A key is a password.

lecture.title: Everyday pictures: a weather API
lecture.say: An API is a menu. The key is a membership card: never print it in a log and never commit it to a repository.

lecture.title: An API answers in JSON; json.loads turns it into data
lecture.say: A web API answers in JSON text. Json.loads turns it into dictionaries and lists. Read the data one key or position at a time.

lecture.title: The API gives Kelvin; the program converts
lecture.say: The weather API reports Kelvin. Subtract 273.15 for Celsius, then convert to Fahrenheit. The chapter prints 12.3 and 54.1 for 285.44 Kelvin.

lecture.title: An endpoint, its parameters and a secret key
lecture.say: An endpoint is one address of a service. The key is a parameter, so it travels inside the address. Log the address only with the key hidden.

lecture.title: Part 4: Reading HTML
lecture.say: Part four. HTML is a tree of elements. We list its tags, pick elements by a path, avoid regular expressions, and resolve the links that a page holds. Two of the book's projects use these steps.

lecture.title: Everyday pictures: reading HTML
lecture.say: Seven pictures for reading HTML. The selector is an address for an element, and the developer tools show the boxes inside a page.

lecture.title: Everyday pictures: picking things out of a page
lecture.say: Select, get_text and get are the three moves of Beautiful Soup. The two projects use them to open results and to walk back through a comic series.

lecture.title: HTML is nested tags with attributes
lecture.say: HTML is nested tags with attributes. The parser calls a method for each opening tag. Predict which tag has no attributes.

lecture.title: Pick elements by a path, read their text and attributes
lecture.say: Beautiful Soup is not in the standard library, so ElementTree plays its part. The same three moves: select, get text, get an attribute.

lecture.title: Story: Beautiful Soup, for pages somebody else wrote, 2004
lecture.say: Leonard Richardson has kept Beautiful Soup since 2004. His promise: you did not write that awful page, you only want data from it. That is why we use a parser and not a regular expression.

lecture.title: Do not read HTML with a regular expression
lecture.say: The pattern needs href right after the tag name. The second link has a class first. A parser reads attributes by name and finds both.

lecture.title: Practice program: link verification
lecture.say: Practice program. Make links absolute, drop the fragment, skip other sites and count each page once. Predict how many pages remain.

lecture.title: Project 8: the image and the Prev link of a comic page
lecture.say: Project eight relies on the page structure of the comic site. The image address begins with two slashes, so urljoin borrows the scheme. Prev leads to the previous comic.

lecture.title: Project 7: open the first results in browser tabs
lecture.say: Project seven. Select all result links, keep the first few and open each one. A recording stand-in replaces the real open call.

lecture.title: Part 5: Driving a browser
lecture.say: Part five. Some pages are written by a script after the download. Then only a real browser helps: Selenium or Playwright. We build small stand-ins to see how they behave.

lecture.title: Everyday pictures: driving a browser with Selenium
lecture.say: Selenium drives a real browser from outside. Find_element and find_elements differ in what they do when nothing matches.

lecture.title: Everyday pictures: driving a browser with Playwright
lecture.say: Playwright starts with a context manager, opens a page, goes to an address and uses locators that wait. Browsers are installed by a second step.

lecture.title: Why a download is not enough: pages built by a script
lecture.say: The downloaded source holds an empty element and a script. A parser cannot read what the script writes. A real browser can, even headless.

lecture.title: Story: Selenium began as a test runner for a timesheet, 2004
lecture.say: Selenium began in 2004 at ThoughtWorks as a test tool for a timesheet application. Later it merged with WebDriver. The browser is driven from outside, which is why a driver is needed.

lecture.title: Selenium: find_element fails, find_elements does not
lecture.say: A stand-in for the Selenium driver. Find_elements returns a list that may be empty, find_element returns the first match and fails when there is none.

lecture.title: Playwright: start, new page, goto, locator
lecture.say: The same four steps as the chapter's program: start, new page, goto, locator. The real program also launches a browser first.

lecture.title: Story: Playwright reached Python on 30 September 2020
lecture.say: Arjun Attam announced Playwright for Python in preview on 30 September 2020. Its first promise is automatic waiting, which our last example imitates. Ask students why waiting matters on a slow page.

lecture.title: Interacting with a page: wait until the element is there
lecture.say: Playwright looks again until the element is ready. Selenium's find_element looks once. Predict the result with five looks and with two.

lecture.title: Which tool for which page?
lecture.say: Choose the tool by the page in front of the program. Webbrowser to show it, requests to fetch it, an API when there is one, a parser for static HTML, a browser driver only when a script builds the page.

lecture.title: Current Python and today's web change more
lecture.say: Python and the tools move on. The robots parser reads wildcard rules since Python 3.14.5. Selenium finds its driver by itself. Playwright needs a second install step. Run what the book printed, then check what changed.

lecture.title: Summary
lecture.say: Five sentences to keep. The chart counts the code examples in each part of this deck.

lecture.title: Practice Questions
lecture.say: Four drills and a project. Predict first, then run what you can on the page. Ask students to explain each answer in one sentence.

lecture.title: Resources: where to go next
lecture.say: Start with the book chapter, then the Python documentation, the documents of the four tools and the two protocol texts. The stories link to first-hand sources. Choose one link and read it before the next class.

stories.title: The first spider counted 130 web sites in June 1993
stories.story: Matthew Gray wrote the World Wide Web Wanderer at MIT in the spring of 1993 to traverse the Web systematically and collect sites; he was at first motivated mainly to discover new sites, because the Web was still a relatively small place. As the Web grew rapidly his purpose turned to charting its growth, and his own report counts 130 Web sites in June 1993, 623 in December 1993, 2,738 in June 1994 and 23,500 in June 1995, with 100,000 by January 1996, when the regular traversals ended. He describes the Wanderer as the first automated Web agent, or spider. It did what the chapter's comic downloader does at toy scale: fetch a page, find its links, follow them, and repeat.
stories.lesson: A crawler is a program that follows links; the first one counted 130 sites
stories.source: Matthew Gray, 'Internet Growth and Statistics: Credits and Background', www.mit.edu/~mkgray/net/background.html (spring 1993; traversals from June 1993 to January 1996; first automated Web agent or spider); Matthew Gray, 'Measuring the Growth of the Web, June 1993 to June 1995', stuff.mit.edu/people/mkgray/growth/ (the table of Web sites per month, copyright 1995).

stories.title: A courtesy file for robots, agreed on 30 June 1994
stories.who: Martijn Koster and the robot authors of the robots mailing list
stories.where: The robots mailing list at Nexor, and the Web
stories.story: Martijn Koster wrote down A Standard for Robot Exclusion, a text that records a consensus reached on 30 June 1994 on the robots mailing list at nexor.co.uk between the majority of robot authors. It answered what the text itself reports: in 1993 and 1994 some robots had swamped servers with rapid-fire requests or retrieved the same files repeatedly, and others had wandered into deep virtual trees and cgi scripts with side effects such as voting. The remedy was one file at the URL /robots.txt, which a robot reads first. The document says plainly that it is not an official standard, is not enforced by anybody, and that nothing guarantees that every robot will use it. The method became RFC 9309 in September 2022, with Koster, Illyes, Zeller and Sassman as authors, and Python's urllib.robotparser read its wildcard rules only from release 3.14.5 on 10 May 2026.
stories.lesson: Robots.txt is a 1994 courtesy, not a lock: honour it
stories.source: 'A Standard for Robot Exclusion', Martijn Koster, www.robotstxt.org/orig.html (consensus of 30 June 1994 on the robots mailing list, robots-request@nexor.co.uk; not an official standard; not enforced by anybody); RFC 9309, Robots Exclusion Protocol, Koster, Illyes, Zeller and Sassman, IETF, September 2022 (a method originally defined by Martijn Koster in 1994; rules are not a form of access authorization); Python 3.14 changelog, 3.14.5 final, released 2026-05-10, gh-138907, docs.python.org/3.14/whatsnew/changelog.html.

stories.title: Beautiful Soup, for the awful pages somebody else wrote, since 2004
stories.story: Leonard Richardson's page for Beautiful Soup greets the reader with the line 'You didn't write that awful page. You're just trying to get some data out of it', and says that since 2004 the library has been saving programmers hours or days of work on quick-turnaround screen scraping projects. Wikipedia adds, marking the point as needing a citation, that the name comes from the poem Beautiful Soup in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland and plays on tag soup, the term for poorly structured HTML. Beautiful Soup 3 was the official release line from May 2006 to March 2012, and the line the chapter installs as beautifulsoup4 is the fourth. On 12 October 2026 the author's page named 4.14.3 of 30 November 2025 as the current release, while pip installed 4.15.0 for this chapter: a library's own page can lag its releases.

stories.title: Selenium began in 2004 as a test runner for a timesheet application
stories.who: Jason Huggins, with Paul Gross and Jie Tina Wang
stories.story: The Selenium project's own history says the story starts in 2004 at ThoughtWorks in Chicago, where Jason Huggins, helped by Paul Gross and Jie Tina Wang, built the Core mode as JavaScriptTestRunner to test an internal Time and Expenses application written in Python and Plone. Colleagues liked its immediate visual feedback, and soon afterwards Paul Hammant saw the demo and began the talks about open sourcing it and about a driven mode that could be used over the wire from a language of one's choice. Separately, Simon Stewart at ThoughtWorks built WebDriver, which did not rely on JavaScript but had a client for each browser coded from scratch, and the two projects were merged. The webdriver.Firefox() call of the chapter descends from that merge.

stories.title: Playwright reached Python in preview on 30 September 2020
stories.who: Arjun Attam and the Playwright team at Microsoft
stories.story: On 30 January 2020 InfoQ reported that Microsoft had announced Playwright as an alternative to Puppeteer, quoting the team: the same team that originally built Puppeteer at Google, which had since moved on. On 30 September 2020 Arjun Attam, a program manager, announced Playwright for Python in preview on the Microsoft for Python Developers blog, saying that the JavaScript version had been released earlier in the year. The post's first claim is reliable, timeout-free automation: Playwright automatically waits for the UI to be ready, with an event-driven design that listens to browser events such as DOM changes, network requests and page navigations. That is the auto-waiting of the chapter, including the thirty seconds a mistyped selector costs.
